Setting from the Workshop bible row (the catalog's lld entries carry no setting), worded to honour w02's next field ("a student residence's lift in exam week, and state machines"). Sources: Harel's abstract is quoted from the Recurse Center page that reproduces it, because the publisher's page and the Weizmann copies would not load.
title: The Lift That Forgot
setting: a student hall of residence's lift in exam week

post.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
post.title: I finish my late great-aunt's machines at night. The lift program I finished for a student hall left a call button lit on floor 6 while the lift sat idle at floor 1 for 11 minutes. Its own log saw the press.

blocks.text: My great-aunt Winifrith Torvaine built coin machines and clockwork figures for sixty years, and wrote small programs for local firms in her last ten. She died in the spring, leaving me her workshop of unfinished machines, each with a paper work order tied on with string. I program on night shifts and finish them at night.

This one came from Quorrie House, a student hall with eight floors and one lift. It asked for a new controller: the program that decides where the lift goes next. Each landing has one call button, and the lift has a button per floor. A button's light is wired to the button, not the program: it stays lit until the doors open at that floor.

Winifrith's notebook drew the lift as six circles: idle, moving up, moving down, doors opening, doors open, doors closing. The lift is always in exactly one, like a traffic light showing one colour. Each circle is called a state. Anything that happens to the lift, a press, reaching a floor, the doors finishing, is called an event. Beside the circles she wrote: *A knock nobody answers is still a knock.*

When an event arrives, the program first looks at the current state, then does what that state says about the event, and last may move the lift to a new state. That move is called a transition. I coded each state's reactions to the events I expected. Each line below is a state, an event and the reaction; *call f* is a press for floor f, and the list holds floors still to visit:

idle           call f: list f, go
moving         call f: list f
               floor f: stop if listed
doors opening  call f: list f
               opened: doors open
doors open     call f: list f
               5 s up: doors closing
doors closing  call here: open again
               shut: nearest listed, or idle
The doors take 2 seconds (s) to open, stay open 5 s and take 2 s to close; the lift takes 4 s a floor. It went in on Saturday. Exam week began on Monday.
The controller writes a log, one line per call or change of state: the time, the state, the event and what it did. A dash means it did nothing. Early Wednesday:

02:13:40  idle           call 4   doors opening
02:13:42  doors opening  opened   doors open
02:13:42  doors open     call 1   list 1
02:13:47  doors open     5 s up   doors closing
02:13:49  doors closing  shut     moving down
02:14:01  moving down    floor 1  doors opening
02:14:03  doors opening  opened   doors open
02:14:08  doors open     5 s up   doors closing
02:14:09  doors closing  call 6   -
02:14:10  doors closing  shut     idle
02:25:10  idle           call 6   moving up

Ofeliya, from floor 4, had ridden down and gone out. At 02:14:09 Zlatoslava, on floor 6, pressed the call button. The light came on; the lift stayed at floor 1. At 02:21 Zlatoslava phoned Mr Quaintance, the night warden, who said to press again. At 02:25:10 they did, and the lift set off at once.
The button remembered the press. The program never heard it.
Mr Quaintance emailed me the log at 07:00. By day, he says, students jab buttons twice. Zlatoslava waited 11 minutes 23 s for the doors, on a dark landing. What should I change before tonight?

blocks.label: lift_log_0213_redrawn.png

diagram.aria: Forty seconds from 02:13:40. The doors move from 02:13:40 to 02:13:42, are open until 02:13:47 and close until 02:13:49. The lift moves from 02:13:49 to 02:14:01. The doors open from 02:14:01 to 02:14:03, stay open until 02:14:08 and close until 02:14:10. The call from floor 6 arrives at 02:14:09, inside the closing. Floor 6's light is on from 02:14:09 to the end. The lift is idle from 02:14:10.

blocks.caption: I redrew the log as a timeline, 40 seconds from 02:13:40. Ofeliya's trip: the doors open and close at floor 4, the lift moves down from 02:13:49 to 02:14:01, and the doors open and close at floor 1. The call from floor 6 lands at 02:14:09, one second before the doors finish closing. From 02:14:10 the light is on and the lift is idle, and it stays idle until the second press at 02:25:10.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: What Winifrith drew has a name: a state machine, a set of states and the events that move a thing between them. Try this with your listing. Draw a grid, called a transition table: one row per state, one column per kind of event, and in each square write what your code does. Leave a square blank where your code says nothing. Then lay your log beside it. Which square was the 02:14:09 line standing in? And what did your program keep, anywhere, of that press? The button kept it. Did anything else?

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Six states and five kinds of event: call, floor reached, doors opened, 5 s up, doors shut. Thirty squares. Most of my blanks can't happen; the doors can't finish opening while the lift is idle. One can: a call from another floor while the doors close. That square is blank. The press went nowhere, not even onto the list.

comments.author: u/first_come_zephaniah
comments.text: The real bug is your nearest-floor rule. I've watched lifts like that: a lone call far away loses to every nearer one, again and again. Serve calls strictly in the order they were pressed, first come, first served, like a queue at a post office. Then nobody ever waits behind someone who pressed after them. Fair is simple.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: There were no other calls at 02:14. But Mr Quaintance says the 08:41 rush on exam mornings is when people moan about waiting. He remembers a lift engineer's rule too: keep going the way you're going while a listed floor lies ahead, then turn back.

comments.author: u/fresh_start_gautrek
comments.text: Controllers hang. The one on our depot gate did. Restart it every 10 minutes: switch the program off and on, and it starts again fresh, idle, with an empty list. Then no lift can sit there forgotten for longer than that.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Mr Quaintance asked if I could do what the hall's old controller did before it wore out. It ran a loop: a part of a program that repeats the same steps over and over. Every second it read every button, whatever the state, and added any lit floor to the list.

reply.prompt: The hall will be up all night again. What should Odgerel change before tonight? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Restart the controller every 10 minutes, so it starts fresh from idle with an empty list.
options.verdict: A restart can't recall a lost call
options.part2: Before it went in, I replayed Wednesday night on Winifrith's workbench with a restart every 10 minutes on the clock. At 02:20:00 it restarted: idle at floor 1, an empty list, and floor 6's light still on. A restart starts from nothing, and the call had never been kept, so there was nothing to get back. Zlatoslava still waited for the second press at 02:25:10: 683 s, 11 minutes 23 s, in all. Monday's 08:41 rush, replayed from the hall's log, came out exactly as before, with the student on floor 8 waiting 135 s. It went into the hall on Thursday anyway. That week a lone call landed in a closing window again and sat lit until its student pressed twice. And one restart caught the lift between floors with a student inside: it stopped at the next floor and forgot where they were going, so they had to press their floor again.
options.senior: A restart clears what a program remembers; it cannot add what the program never kept. The call was lost the moment the doors-closing state ignored it, so restarting treats a hang that never happened and leaves the real hole. It also adds a new danger: every restart throws away the whole list, including the floors of people already in the lift. Restarts are for programs that stop answering. This one answered every event it had a square for, and simply had no square for this one.

options.text: Add a loop that reads every button once a second, whatever the state, and lists any lit floor.
options.verdict: Trade-off: nothing lost, a second late
options.part2: I added the loop. Every second it reads all 16 buttons, 8 on the landings and 8 in the lift, and lists any lit floor that isn't listed yet, whatever the state. On the workbench, Wednesday night came out right: the loop read floor 6 at 02:14:10, during doors closing, and the doors opened on floor 6 at 02:14:33, 24 s after the press. But every press now waits for the next read, so every trip starts a second late. Monday's 08:41 rush, replayed from the hall's log, left the student on floor 8 waiting 136 s instead of 135, because the nearest-floor rule was unchanged. In the hall, no call has been lost since Thursday. Then Mr Quaintance asked for a key that takes the lift out of service for cleaning, and on the bench I caught the loop listing lit floors anyway. It knows nothing of states, so the new state had to be taught to the loop as well as to the program before the key went in.
options.senior: Reading every button on a timer, whatever the state, does make the program unable to lose a press: the buttons remember, and the loop asks them. That is honest and simple. The cost is up to a second's delay on every call, a loop that runs all night whether anyone is there or not, and a second place where the rules live. The state machine still has its blank square; the loop just walks around it. Every new state or feature now has to be taught to both, and the morning rush is still served nearest floor first.

options.text: Serve calls strictly in the order they were pressed, first come, first served, never nearest.
options.verdict: A fairer order, the same hole
options.part2: I changed one line: the next stop is the first floor on the list, in the order pressed, and the lift stops only there. On the workbench, Wednesday night came out exactly as before. The press at 02:14:09 still reached the doors-closing state, which still had no reaction, and Zlatoslava waited 683 s, 11 minutes 23 s. Monday's 08:41 rush, replayed from the hall's log, was kinder to the student on floor 8, who waited 32 s instead of 135. But the lift zigzagged past floors that had calls waiting: 26 floors travelled instead of 24, and the seven students' waits added up to 538 s instead of 423. The student on floor 2 waited 113 s. It went into the hall on Thursday, and that week a lone call landed in a closing window again and sat lit until its student pressed twice.
options.senior: Choosing who goes next was never the bug: the call was lost before any rule could choose it. Strict pressed order does stop a far floor from being passed over again and again, but it ignores where the lift is, so it criss-crosses the building and, in a rush, most people wait longer. Fix the lost call in the state machine first, then choose a rule that is both fair and efficient.

options.text: Fill every square of the table, list calls in any state, and serve one way, then back.
options.part2: I drew the table: six states down the side, five events across, thirty squares, and filled every one. Squares that can't happen now say so, and write a log line if they ever do. The doors-closing square for a call from another floor now says: list it, and go once the doors are shut. Then I changed the next-stop rule: keep going the way you are going while a listed floor lies ahead, then turn back. On the workbench, Wednesday night: the press at 02:14:09 was kept, the doors shut at 02:14:10, and they opened on floor 6 at 02:14:32, 23 s after the press. Monday's 08:41 rush, replayed from the hall's log: the seven students' waits added up to 245 s instead of 423, the longest was 56 s instead of 135, the lift travelled 14 floors instead of 24, and everyone was at floor 1 by 08:43:01. One cost: with one button per landing, the student on floor 4 got in while the lift was going up and rode to floor 8 and back, 107 s in the lift instead of 21. It went in on Thursday. No call has been lost since, and Mr Quaintance is asking about up and down buttons on each landing.
options.senior: A state machine is only as good as its emptiest square. Write it as a table and every state must say what it does with every event, even if the answer is 'keep it for later' or 'can't happen, log it'; a blank then shows up in review instead of on a landing at 02:14. A list that every state can add to separates remembering a call from serving it. The next-stop rule is then a separate choice: going one way while there is work ahead, then turning back, usually keeps every wait within about one trip up and down, and travels far less than first come, first served.

sim.title: Replay the lift on Winifrith's workbench
sim.lede: You're Odgerel at the workbench, replaying the hall's log through the controller. Two scenes: Wednesday from 02:13:30, before Ofeliya's press, with the lift idle at floor 4; and Monday's first exam morning from 08:40:55, with the lift idle at floor 1 and seven students, one on each of floors 2 to 8, pressing between 08:41:00 and 08:41:52, all going down to floor 1. The doors take 2 s to open, stay open 5 s and take 2 s to close; the lift takes 4 s a floor. A wait runs from a press until the doors finish opening at that floor. Pick a design: as built; restarted every 10 minutes (at 02:20:00 in the night scene; none falls in the morning); calls served in the order pressed; a loop that reads all 16 buttons every second; or every square of the table filled, with calls served one way, then back. The table shows what each state does with each event, and outlines the square each step used.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press step until 02:14:09 and watch the outlined square in the doors-closing row. Play the rest and read floor 6's wait. Try the restart and the order pressed: still 683 s. Try the loop, then the full table: 24 s and 23 s. Then switch to the morning scene and compare the longest wait, all waits added up, and floors travelled for each design.

explain.oneLine: Nothing broke and nothing hung. The doors-closing state had no reaction to a call from another floor, so the press at 02:14:09 was dropped; the light, wired to the button, stayed on, and the lift went idle with an empty list.

steps.title: Six states, and the events that move between them.
steps.text: A state machine describes a thing that is always in exactly one state and changes state only when an event arrives. Winifrith's lift has six states: idle, moving up, moving down, doors opening, doors open, doors closing. Each event is handled in three steps. First, the program looks at the current state. Second, it runs that state's reaction to the event, such as adding a floor to the list. Third, it may make a transition to a new state. What can go wrong is the second step: if the state has no reaction written for that event, nothing runs, and nothing complains.

steps.title: One blank square, two seconds wide.
steps.text: Odgerel coded each state's reaction to the events expected there. Doors closing expected two: the doors finishing, and a call on the same floor, which opens them again. A call from another floor was never written down. Here is the night in order. At 02:14:08 the doors at floor 1 start closing. At 02:14:09 Zlatoslava's press arrives; the state is doors closing, the square is blank, so the program does nothing. At 02:14:10 the doors shut; the program looks at its list, finds it empty, and goes idle. Only a press inside those 2 s is lost, which is why it took a lone call at night to hit it.

steps.title: The button remembered; the program didn't.
steps.text: Winifrith's line, a knock nobody answers is still a knock, reads plainly now: the press was the knock, the blank square was nobody answering, and the lit button went on knocking. The light is wired to the button, so it said the call was taken. The program's list said nothing was waiting. Two records disagreed, and only the program moves the lift. By day a second press always came, from the same student or the next one, and landed in a state that listens, so nobody noticed. A restart can't help: it empties the list, and the call was never on it. A loop that reads every button each second does catch it, a second later, by asking the buttons instead of fixing the state.

steps.title: Fill the table, and keep every call.
steps.text: Write the state machine as a transition table: a row per state, a column per event, and every square filled. The answer may be an action, 'keep it for later', or 'can't happen, so log it', but never blank. Then make the list of stops the one place a call is remembered, and let every state add to it. The doors-closing square for a call elsewhere becomes 'list it'; when the doors shut, the lift goes. A test that sends every event to every state then checks all thirty squares in a few lines, and the next new state shows its blank row before anyone stands on a landing.

steps.title: Then choose who goes next.
steps.text: Three rules for the next stop. Nearest first travels little, but a far floor can wait while nearer calls keep arriving: on Monday's rush the student on floor 8 waited 135 s. First come, first served is fair in order but criss-crosses the building: 26 floors travelled and 538 s of waiting in all. One way, then back keeps going while a listed floor lies ahead and turns only when none does, so a call waits at most about one trip up and down: 14 floors, 245 s in all, longest 56 s. Its cost with one button per landing: a student going down may ride up first.

diagram.aria: The fix, replayed for Wednesday night. The call for floor 6 at 02:14:09 arrives during doors closing. The full state table's square for doors closing and a call elsewhere says list it. The list of stops holds 6. When the doors shut at 02:14:10 the next-stop rule, one way then back, sends the lift up 5 floors in 20 s, and the doors open on floor 6 at 02:14:32, 23 s after the press.

explain.caption: The fix, replayed for Wednesday night. The press at 02:14:09 still arrives while the doors close, but now that square has an answer: list it. The list is the one place a call is remembered, so when the doors shut at 02:14:10 the next-stop rule finds floor 6 and the lift goes up 5 floors in 20 s. The doors open on floor 6 at 02:14:32, 23 s after the press.

fix.title: The fix: every square filled, calls kept in any state, one way then back
fix.text: Write the controller's states and events as a table, six states by five events, and fill all thirty squares. Where a square can't happen, write that it can't, and log a line if it ever does. Make the list of stops the only place a call is remembered, and let every state add to it; in doors closing, a call from another floor is listed and served once the doors shut. Change the next-stop rule to keep going the way the lift is going while a listed floor lies ahead, then turn back. Add a test that sends every event to every state and checks the square's answer, so the next new state cannot ship with a blank row.

limits: One call button per landing can't tell the lift which way a student wants to go, so one way, then back sometimes carries someone the wrong way first: on Monday's rush the student on floor 4 rode up to floor 8 and back, 107 s in the lift instead of 21. Up and down buttons on each landing fix that.

A full table is only as right as its squares. 'Can't happen' squares must log when they do happen, and every new state or event adds a whole row or column to fill; the test that walks every square is what keeps the next blank from shipping.

One way, then back keeps waits bounded, not short. With one lift, a call just behind it waits for a full trip up and back. In a busier building the next step is more lifts, or giving lifts their own floors, which is a different decision.

head: Design
Good
Bad
rows: As built: blank square, nearest floor next
Little travel when calls are near each other.
A call during doors closing is dropped: 683 s on Wednesday. A far floor can wait: 135 s on Monday.
Clears a program that has truly hung.
Can't bring back a call never kept: still 683 s. Throws away the floors of people in the lift.
No floor is passed over again and again: floor 8 waits 32 s.
The hole stays: 683 s. Zigzags: 26 floors and 538 s of waiting on Monday.
Loop reads every button each second
No press is ever lost: 24 s on Wednesday.
Every call a second late; runs all night; the rules live in two places; nearest-first unchanged.
Full table, list in any state, one way then back
No dropped call: 23 s. Monday: 245 s of waiting, longest 56 s, 14 floors.
With one button per landing some ride the wrong way first: 107 s in the lift for floor 4.

explain.seniorTake: Most state bugs are not wrong answers but missing ones: a state that was never asked what it does with an event. Draw the machine as a table, fill every square, and make 'can't happen' an answer that logs. Keep what must be remembered, a call, an order, a request, in one place that every state can add to, separate from the rule that decides what to serve next. Then choose that rule on purpose. Nearest first is quick until a far request starves; first come, first served is fair and slow; going one way while there is work ahead, then turning back, is the old elevator answer for a reason. And when two records disagree, like a lit button and an empty list, believe neither until you know which one moves the lift.

realWorld.title: Harel, 1987: statecharts
realWorld.text: David Harel's paper "Statecharts: a visual formalism for complex systems" (Science of Computer Programming, 1987) opens its abstract: "We present a broad extension of the conventional formalism of state machines and state diagrams, that is relevant to the specification and design of complex discrete-event systems, such as multi-computer real-time systems, communication protocols and digital control units." The abstract is quoted here as the Recurse Center's page reproduces it.

realWorld.title: Statecharts add three things
realWorld.text: The same abstract: "Our diagrams, which we call statecharts, extend conventional state-transition diagrams with essentially three elements, dealing, respectively, with the notions of hierarchy, concurrency and communication." A lift with a separate door state inside each floor stop is the kind of nesting that hierarchy describes.

realWorld.title: Nearest first can starve
realWorld.text: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, on scheduling a disk's requests, describes nearest-first as shortest-seek-time-first (SSTF) and warns of starvation: with "a steady stream of requests to the inner track, where the head currently is positioned", "Requests to any other tracks would then be ignored completely by a pure SSTF approach."

realWorld.title: The elevator algorithm
realWorld.text: The same chapter: SCAN "simply moves back and forth across the disk servicing requests in order across the tracks", and "the SCAN algorithm (and its cousins) is sometimes referred to as the elevator algorithm, because it behaves like an elevator which is either going up or down and not just servicing requests to floors based on which floor is closer." Of disks it adds: "In disks, it just prevents starvation."

realWorld.title: LOOK: turn back when nothing lies ahead
realWorld.text: Wikipedia's LOOK algorithm article describes the variant this case uses: "If no requests are pending in the direction of head movement, then the disk head traversal will be reversed to the opposite direction and requests on the other direction can be served."

asked: Design the controller for a single lift.
How would you model the lift's states and events?
Which rule would you use to pick the next stop, and why?
interview.answer: Model the lift as a state machine. States: idle, moving up, moving down, doors opening, doors open, doors closing. Events: a call from a landing or from inside, reaching a floor, doors opened, the open timer running out, doors shut. Write it as a transition table and fill every square, including 'can't happen, log it', and test every square, because the classic bug is a state with no answer for an event, such as a call arriving while the doors close. Keep calls in one list of stops that every state can add to, so remembering a call is separate from serving it. For the next stop, nearest first travels least but can starve a far floor; first come, first served is fair but zigzags; I'd go one way while any listed floor lies ahead, then turn back, the LOOK form of the elevator algorithm, which bounds waits to about one round trip. With one button per landing some riders go the wrong way first, so I'd ask for up and down buttons. For several lifts, I'd add a dispatcher that assigns each call to one lift, using the same rule inside each.

terms.def: The workshop Winifrith Torvaine left Odgerel, full of half-finished coin machines and automata, each with a paper work order and a program file to match.
A paper slip saying what a client wants made or mended. Each of Winifrith's unfinished machines has one tied to it with string.
The student hall of residence in this story: eight floors, one lift, and Mr Quaintance as night warden.
A building where university students live, usually with shared kitchens and a warden on duty.
The person on duty in a hall of residence overnight. Students phone them when something goes wrong.
The floor area outside the lift doors on each floor, where the call button is.
The button on a landing that asks the lift to come. At Quorrie House there is one per landing, and its light is wired to the button itself.
The program that decides where the lift goes next. It does not run the lift's safety parts, such as door edges and brakes, which are separate.
Which one of a fixed set of situations a thing is in right now, like a traffic light showing one colour. The lift has six: idle, moving up, moving down, doors opening, doors open, doors closing.
Anything that happens to the machine that the program must react to: a button press, reaching a floor, the doors finishing opening or closing, a timer running out.
A move from one state to another, made because of an event. Doors closing to idle, when the doors shut and the list is empty, is one.
A description of a thing as a set of states and the events that move it between them. It is always in exactly one state.
A state machine written as a grid: a row per state, a column per event, and in each square what happens. A blank square is a question nobody answered.
The floors the controller still has to visit. A call is remembered only if it is on this list.
A program's written record of what it did, one line per happening, with the time. The controller logs every call and every change of state.
Short for seconds. The doors take 2 s to open and 2 s to close; the lift takes 4 s a floor.
The 2 s while the doors close. In the program as built, a call from another floor arriving in this window was dropped.
A press the program received but did nothing with, so it was never put on the list. The button's light stays on anyway.
Pick the listed floor closest to the lift as the next stop. Little travel, but a far floor can wait while nearer calls keep arriving.
Serve requests strictly in the order they arrived, like a queue at a post office. Fair in order, but a lift doing it criss-crosses the building.
Keep going the way the lift is going while any listed floor lies ahead, stopping at each; turn back only when none does. Known as LOOK, a form of the elevator algorithm.
When a request keeps being passed over because others keep looking better, so it waits far longer than anyone meant it to.
A rule from disk scheduling: move back and forth across all the requests, serving them in order along the way, like a lift going up then down.
A form of the elevator algorithm that turns back as soon as no request lies ahead, instead of always going to the end.
Short for shortest seek time first: the disk version of the nearest-floor rule, which always serves the nearest request next.
An old-style hard disk stores data in rings called tracks; a moving arm, the head, travels across them to read. Choosing which request it serves next is disk scheduling.
Choosing which waiting job to serve next. Here: which listed floor the lift visits next.
Switching a program off and on so it starts again from the beginning: here, idle with an empty list. Anything it only remembered is lost.
A part of a program that repeats the same steps over and over, such as reading every button once a second.
David Harel's 1987 extension of state diagrams, adding states inside states, states running side by side, and communication between them.
A small program that runs your code with known inputs and checks the answers. A test can send every event to every state and check each square.
Winifrith's bench, where Odgerel replays a stretch of the hall's log through a design before it goes into the lift.
From a press until the doors finish opening at that floor. Zlatoslava's was 683 s: 02:14:09 to 02:25:32.
The first exam morning, from the hall's log: seven students, one on each of floors 2 to 8, pressing between 08:41:00 and 08:41:52, all going to floor 1.

atWork: Look for the state machines already hiding in your systems: an order that goes placed, paid, packed, shipped; a payment that is pending, settled or refunded; a support ticket; a phone app's connection that is online, offline or reconnecting. Read-only access to the code is enough. Find where the state is kept and every place that handles an event, then draw the table: a row per state, a column per event. For each blank square, ask what happens if that event arrives now, such as a refund request while a payment is still pending or a cancel while an order is being packed. Many teams find their worst bugs in exactly those squares, because the code quietly does nothing and some other record, like the lit button here, says the request was taken. Fill every square, even with 'can't happen, log it', and add a test that sends every event to every state. Then look at anything that picks what to serve next, a job queue or a dispatcher, and check whether it can starve the far end.

recall.prompt: A launderette's washing machines run a program with the states idle, filling, washing, draining and spinning. The cancel button is handled in filling and washing. On Saturday a customer pressed cancel while the drum was draining; the machine went on to spin for 12 minutes, and the cancel light stayed on the whole time. What went wrong, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The draining state has no reaction to cancel, so the press was dropped while the button's light said it was taken
Write the state machine as a table where every state says what it does with every event
Make the button and the program agree: act on the press, keep it for later, or refuse it visibly, and test every square

recall.model: The draining state has no reaction to cancel, so the press was dropped: nothing ran, nothing complained, and the light, wired to the button, kept saying the cancel was taken. Write the machine as a transition table, a row for each state and a column for each event, so every state must say what it does with every event; the blank square in the draining row then shows up in review. For cancel while draining, either act on it (finish draining, then stop instead of spinning) or keep it for later and act when draining ends. If you must refuse it, turn the light off so the customer knows. Then add a test that sends every event to every state and checks each square.

recall.prompt: The lift is at floor 4 and going up. Calls are listed for floors 2, 6, 8 and 5, pressed in that order. Served one way, then back, in which order does it visit them?
recall.why: Going up from floor 4, it serves every listed floor ahead in the order it reaches them: 5, 6, then 8. Nothing lies further up, so it turns back and serves 2. The pressed order (2, 6, 8, 5) is first come, first served, and 5, 2, 6, 8 is the nearest-floor rule.

recall.prompt: Your team's warehouse robot fetches boxes from shelves along one long aisle, numbered 1 to 40. One colleague says always go to the closest waiting shelf: it's the fastest. Another says first come, first served is fairest. In a busy hour, what goes wrong with each, and what rule would you use?

keyIdeas.idea: Closest-first can starve a far shelf while nearer requests keep arriving
First come, first served zigzags along the aisle, so the robot travels more and most requests wait longer
Go one way serving every request ahead, then turn back (the elevator algorithm); waits stay bounded

recall.model: Closest-first travels little, but in a busy hour it can starve the far end: while requests keep arriving near the robot, a box at shelf 40 is passed over again and again. First come, first served is fair in order, but it ignores where the robot is, so it zigzags along the aisle; it travels more and most requests wait longer. Use the elevator algorithm in its LOOK form: go one way, serving every request ahead in the order you reach it, and turn back only when none lies ahead. Every request then waits at most about one sweep there and back, and the travel stays low.

recall.prompt: Instead of fixing the doors-closing square, a loop reads every button once a second, whatever the state, and lists any lit floor. What does it give, and what does it cost?
options: No press is ever lost, but every call waits for the next read and the rules now live in two places
Calls are served sooner than when the program reacts to each press
It adds the missing reaction to the doors-closing row of the table
It stops a far floor from waiting behind nearer calls
recall.why: The buttons remember every press, so a loop that asks them can't lose one. But each call now waits up to a second for the next read, the loop runs all night, and every new state must be taught to both the loop and the program. The blank square is still blank, and the next-stop rule is unchanged.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. The table has held: not one lost call since. Last week Quorrie House asked for a cleaner's key that takes the lift out of service while the floor is wet. I added a seventh state, out of service, and filled its row; for a call it says: no reaction, the lift mustn't move. On Sunday the cleaner turned the key back at 05:40. A student on floor 3 had pressed at 05:31. The light was still on at 05:40, and the lift stayed idle at floor 1 until they pressed again at 05:52.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the student on floor 3 have to press twice, and what should the out-of-service row say for a call?

keyIdeas.idea: It is the same drop again: a filled square that says 'no reaction' still throws the call away while the light stays on
The square should keep the call for later: list it, and serve it once the lift is back in service
Or refuse it visibly, turning the light off or showing the lift is out of service, so the button and the program agree

coldCase.model: It's the same drop in a new square. Filling a square is not enough when the answer is 'no reaction': the call at 05:31 was thrown away, the light stayed on, and when the key turned back at 05:40 the list was empty, so the lift went idle and the student had to press again. Not moving the lift is right; forgetting the call is not. The out-of-service square for a call should say: list it, and keep it for later, so it is served once the lift is back in service. If the hall would rather refuse calls while the floor is wet, refuse them visibly: turn the light off and show an out-of-service sign, so the button and the program agree.
